steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on safe human-robot collaboration that uses learning to pick among multiple backup control barrier functions. Cover safety filters and CBFs/BCBFs, the limitations of current multi-backup and preference-based approaches, our LSTM-DNN switching approach and its contributions, and the paper outline.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Safety filters are useful control tools that let a robot stay safe while it is actuated by a controller, or driver, that is potentially unsafe. Safety filters do this by changing the desired control commands as little as possible, and since they deal with real-world robot dynamics and kinodynamic constraints at run time they have become a popular add-on to robot control architectures.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) are a popular way to build safety filters, because they can integrate nonlinear dynamics and also give formal safety guarantees. A safety filter based on CBFs needs a control-invariant set to be defined that ensures safety. But it can be hard to construct such sets when input constraints are taken into account.

Because of this the CBF framework was extended to include actuation capability, like torque limits, by using backup control barrier functions (BCBFs). BCBFs depend on formulating a backup controller, which is designed with the input limits in mind so that it guarantees safety.

Usually the backup controller is a simple saving maneuver, like coming to a stop, turning at a maximum rate, or hovering. If we calculate the future backup trajectory of the system we can analyze the future safety of the robot and put this information into optimization-based controllers like quadratic programs (QPs). So when safety filters are built with the BCBF method, how conservative the system is depends strongly on which backup policy the control engineer chooses.

- Multiple backup strategies
  - help overcome conservativeness of one strategy
  - one work: evaluate BCBF with multiple backup controllers, pick least control intervention; infeasible with many controllers
  - other works: different maneuvers for reachability, switching algorithm; efficient but for fully autonomous systems; no account of human intentions or human's better situational awareness
  - backup strategy fixed, not tunable -> preferred safe behaviors filtered out
- Human preferences in safety filters
  - preference-based learning tunes CBF parameters, quadruped obstacle avoidance; no formal input bounds
  - pbRL must sample trajectories in expected environment; hard with teleoperation (human-in-the-loop)
- Our approach
  - LSTM + DNN learn reward per backup controller; LSTMs used for driver intention/maneuver tracking
  - switching law: largest reward; trained on driver-labeled example trajectories
  - contributions: learned switching law closest to driver preference; larger reachable sets with BCBF guarantees
  - tracked robot experiments
- Organization: II preliminaries; III contributions + architecture; IV hardware; V results; VI conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Safety filters are useful control tools that let a robot stay safe while it is actuated by a controller, or driver, that is potentially unsafe. Safety filters do this by changing the desired control commands as little as possible, and since they deal with real-world robot dynamics and kinodynamic constraints at run time they have become a popular add-on to robot control architectures.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) are a popular way to build safety filters, because they can integrate nonlinear dynamics and also give formal safety guarantees. A safety filter based on CBFs needs a control-invariant set to be defined that ensures safety. But it can be hard to construct such sets when input constraints are taken into account.

Because of this the CBF framework was extended to include actuation capability, like torque limits, by using backup control barrier functions (BCBFs). BCBFs depend on formulating a backup controller, which is designed with the input limits in mind so that it guarantees safety.

Usually the backup controller is a simple saving maneuver, like coming to a stop, turning at a maximum rate, or hovering. If we calculate the future backup trajectory of the system we can analyze the future safety of the robot and put this information into optimization-based controllers like quadratic programs (QPs). So when safety filters are built with the BCBF method, how conservative the system is depends strongly on which backup policy the control engineer chooses.

To deal with this limitation, recent work looks at using multiple backup strategies in the BCBF framework, since multiple strategies can help overcome the conservativeness of one single strategy. In one work an algorithm evaluates the BCBF method with multiple backup controllers, so that the one with the least control intervention can be picked. But when there are many backup controllers this method might be computationally infeasible. Other works propose different maneuvers to increase the reachability of a given backup controller, and a switching algorithm picks a different maneuver if the current one can no longer be performed. This method used multiple backup maneuvers and more computationally efficient ways to solve BCBFs, but it is better suited for fully autonomous systems. In a human-robot interaction context it does not explicitly give a way to take into account the intentions of a human vehicle driver or a human companion. It also does not account for the fact that the human operator might have better situational awareness than the autonomous controller. Even if autonomous selection is sometimes suboptimal, the backup control strategy is often fixed and does not depend on what kind of safety-critical behavior the driver prefers. In general the types of safe behavior that the BCBF uses cannot be tuned, and so potentially preferred safe behaviors get filtered out by the BCBF framework.

There has been impressive previous work on including human preferences in safety filters. For example, one work uses preference-based learning to adapt tuneable parameters of a CBF to user preferences for autonomous obstacle avoidance on a quadruped. But input bounds are not formally considered there, which could lead to infeasibility and so to unsafe trajectories. There has also been work on preference based reinforcement learning (pbRL), but these methods have to sample trajectories within the expected environment. Since drivers of teleoperated systems have to give control inputs at each timestep, trajectory sampling is hard to do because the problem has a human in the loop.

To pick backup controllers intelligently, we propose a system that uses a long short term memory (LSTM) and a deep neural network (DNN) component to learn a reward for each backup controller. LSTMs have been used for real-time tracking of driver intention and maneuvers, and they were shown to be successful at regression and classification tasks with trajectory input. We derive a simple switching law by using the controller with the largest reward in the BCBF framework. The system learns to estimate driver intention by training on example trajectories that are labeled with the correct choice of backup controller, as given by the driver. In our work we show that

- 1. The LSTM-DNN architecture learns a switching law for the BCBF framework with multiple backup controllers effectively, and chooses the controller that is closest to the preference of the driver.

- 2. Our approach increases the reachable sets of the driven robot and keeps the safety guarantees of BCBFs.

We also present experimental implementations of our algorithms on a tracked robot. The experiments show that switching between new and previously formulated backup controllers based on the estimated driver intention can work on real hardware systems.

The paper is organized like this. Section II gives preliminaries on CBFs, BCBFs, and DNNs. Section III presents our contributions, including a description of the system architecture. Section IV presents the implementation of our framework on hardware and Section V discusses the experimental results. Section VI concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Safety filters are useful control tools that allow a robot to remain safe while under actuation from a potentially unsafe controller, or driver. Safety filters do this by minimally affecting the desired control commands, and since they address real-world robot dynamics and kinodynamic constraints in a run-time fashion, they have become a popular add-on to robot control architectures [1,2,3].

Control barrier functions (CBFs) [4] are a popular method for constructing safety filters because they can integrate nonlinear dynamics while providing formal safety guarantees. A CBF-based safety filter requires defining a control-invariant set that ensures safety. However, such sets can be difficult to construct with input constraints in mind [5,6,7,8,9,10,11].

Consequently, the CBF framework has been extended to include actuation capability, such as torque limits, through backup control barrier functions (BCBFs) [12,13,14]. BCBFs rely on formulating a backup controller, which is designed with input limits in mind to guarantee safety.

The backup controller typically involves a simple saving maneuver, such as coming to a stop, turning at a maximum rate, or hovering. By calculating the future backup trajectory of the system, one can analyze the future safety of the robot and incorporate this information into optimization-based controllers like quadratic programs (QPs). Consequently, when safety filters are constructed using the BCBF method, the system’s conservativeness is a strong function of the control engineer’s choice of backup policy.

To address this limitation, recent work examines the use of multiple backup strategies in the BCBF framework, since multiple strategies can help overcome the conservativeness of a single strategy. In [15], an algorithm evaluates the BCBF method with multiple backup controllers, such that the one with the least control intervention can be chosen. However, with many backup controllers, this method could become computationally infeasible. In [16] and [17], different maneuvers are proposed to increase the reachability of a given backup controller, where a switching algorithm chooses a different maneuver if the current maneuver can no longer be performed. While this method used multiple backup maneuvers with more computationally efficient ways of solving BCBFs, it is better suited to fully autonomous systems. In a human-robot interaction context, it does not explicitly provide a way to take into account the intentions of a human vehicle driver or human companion, nor does it account for the fact that the human operator may have better situational awareness than the autonomous controller. Even though autonomous selection may be suboptimal at times, the backup control strategy is often fixed and independent of the driver’s preferred safety-critical behavior. Generally, the types of safe behavior used by the BCBF cannot be tuned, so potentially preferred safe behaviors are filtered out by the BCBF framework.

There has been impressive previous work on including human preferences in safety filters. For instance, in [18], preference-based learning is used to adapt tuneable parameters of a CBF to user preferences for autonomous obstacle avoidance on a quadruped. However, input bounds are not formally considered, which could result in infeasibility and consequently unsafe trajectories. There has also been work on preference based reinforcement learning (pbRL) [19], but these methods must sample trajectories within the expected environment [20]. Since the drivers of teleoperated systems must provide control inputs at each timestep, trajectory sampling becomes difficult due to the human-in-the-loop nature of the problem.

In order to intelligently pick backup controllers, we propose a system that uses a long short term memory (LSTM) and a deep neural network (DNN) component to learn a reward corresponding to each backup controller. LSTMs have been used in real-time driver intention and maneuver tracking and have been shown to be successful at regression and classification tasks with trajectory input [21,22,23]. A simple switching law is derived by using the controller with the largest reward in the BCBF framework. The system learns to estimate driver intention by training on example trajectories labeled with the correct choice of backup controller, as provided by the driver. In our work, we show that

- 1. The LSTM-DNN architecture effectively learns a switching law for the BCBF framework with multiple backup controllers, choosing the controller closest to the driver’s preference.

- 2. Our approach increases the reachable sets of the driven robot while maintaining the safety guarantees of BCBFs.

Moreover, we present experimental implementations of our algorithms on a tracked robot. These experiments demonstrate that switching between new and previously formulated backup controllers based on estimated driver intention can work on actual hardware systems.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II presents preliminaries on CBFs, BCBFs, and DNNs. Section III presents our contributions, including a description of the system architecture. Section IV presents the implementation of our framework on hardware, and Section V discusses experimental results. Section VI concludes the paper.
